Photoredox/copper-catalyzed
gem-diﬂuoroalkylation-cyanation of 1,3-enynes†
Yachen Wang,a Shuai Liub and Yangen Huang
 *a
A photoredox/copper-catalyzed 1,4-difunctionalization of 1,3-
enynes with readily available di ﬂuoroalkylating reagents and
TMSCN was developed. This reaction proceeded at mild con-
ditions, a ﬀording the corresponding di ﬂuoroalkylated allenes in
good yields with high functional-group tolerance and excellent
regioselectivity.
The selective incorporation of gem-difluoroalkyl groups into
drug-like molecules will have a wide impact on the physico-
chemical properties and biological activity of the parent mole-
cules, so the development of e ﬃcient methods for the incor-
poration of gem-difluoroalkyl moieties into organic molecules
has important value for medicinal chemistry and drug devel-
opment.
1 In the past decades, visible-light photoredox catalysis
has been widely used in the preparation of fluorinated com-
pounds.2 In 2016, Qing ’s group disclosed that fluorinated
phosphonium salts 2a could serve as the fluoroalkyl radical
precursors3 (Scheme 1a). Thenceforth fluorinated phos-
phonium salts have been widely applied in various radical
fluoroalkylation reactions.
4 For example, Qing ’s group have
developed a hydrodifluoromethylation of alkenes derived
from oxindoles with (difluoromethyl)triphenylphosphonium
bromide 2b under photoredox catalysis
5 (Scheme 1b).
Dilman’s group have shown that halodifluoromethylated alco-
hols could be accessed from aldehydes and a readily available
gem-difluoroalkylation reagent – phosphobetaine 2c
(Scheme 1c).
6 Meanwhile, Qing ’s group have disclosed visible
light-induced radical gem-difluoromethylation of thiols with
difluoromethyltriphenylphosphonium triflate 2d7 (Scheme 1d)
and difluoro( phenylthio)methylation of 2,3-allenoic acids with
{difluoro( phenylthio)-methyl}triphenylphosphonium triflate
2e (Scheme 1e).
8
Due to the unique structural characteristics, 9 allenes not
only have important physiological and pharmacological activi-
ties, but also show very interesting reactivity and selectivity
during chemical transformations.
10 Allenes are useful inter-
mediates for the synthesis of natural products and drug mole-
cules.
11 In the past few decades, the importance of allene
chemistry has gradually been realized and attracted wide-
spread attention, and methodologies for the synthesis and
transformation of allenes have been well developed.
12
Thereinto, the 1,4-difunctionalization of 1,3-enynes provides a
versatile and e ﬀective method for the synthesis of allenes.
13
The conventional approaches for 1,4-difunctionalization of
1,3-enynes focused on the allenyl anion pathway, in which

only electrophiles can be incorporated into the allene back-
bone in the second step of functionalization. 14 The 1,4-difunc-
tionalization of 1,3-enynes via a radical pathway would comp-
lement conventional approaches for the synthesis of allenes
(Scheme 2a). Three free radical pathways were mainly devel-
oped including low-valence metal such as Cu and Ni catalyzed
single-electron reduction,
15 organic molecule catalysis
(N-heterocyclic carbene) 16 and photocatalyzed single-electron
oxidation or reduction. 17 In 2018, Liu ’s group reported Cu-
catalyzed ligand-controlled radical 1,2- and 1,4-addition of 1,3-
enynes provides access to a variety of CF 3-substituted allenyl
nitriles with Togni-I as CF 3 source.18 In addition to the use of
Togni trifluoromethyl radicals, benzoyl peroxide (BPO), 14 fluor-
oalkylated iodides, 18 NFSI,18,19 NHP ester, 20 cyclobutanone
oxime esters 21 and N-Cbz-N-trifluoromethyl hydroxylamine
reagents17b,22 were applied as radical precursors to achieve the
corresponding radical functionalization/cyanation reaction
under diﬀerent conditions (Scheme 2b).
Inspired by these impressive achievements and recent
advances, we envisioned that the gem-difluoroalkylallenes
could be accessed via photoredox/copper-catalyzed gem-
difluoroalkylation-cyanation of 1,3-enynes from TMSCN
and difluoromethyl/difluoro( phenylthio)methyl phosphonium
reagents (Scheme 2c). Considering the importance of difluor-
oalkyl groups and the potential derivatization of nitrile
group,
23 the incorporation of both of these groups into allene
molecules would be worthwhile.
Our study commenced with oct-1-en-3-yn-2-ylbenzene ( 1a)
as the model substrate, its reactivity with {difluoro( phenylthio)
methyl}triphenylphosphonium triflate ( 2e) and TMSCN under
photoredox/copper dual catalytic systems was investigated
(Table 1). Gratifyingly, the desired 1,4-difunctionalized product
3a was formed in 88% yield by using a catalytic system consist-
ing of fac-Ir( ppy)3 and Cu(MeCN) 4BF4/dtbbpy with NaOAc as
the base in MeCN under irradiation with blue LEDs (entry 1).
None of the 1,2-difunctionalized product could be detected. In
addition, switching MeCN to other solvents including PhCl,
DCE, THF, DMF and EtOAc proved less e ﬀective (entries 2 – 6).
Screening of di ﬀerent copper catalysts revealed that Cu
(MeCN)
4BF4 was optimal (entries 7 – 9). Subsequently, other
bases including NaHCO 3,K 3PO4, MeONa, CsF and NaOAc were
evaluated (see the ESI †), and the best result was achieved
when NaOAc was used as the base (entry 1). After a series of
explorations (see the ESI †), it was found that the most appro-
priate ratio of reactants 1a/2e is 1.5/1 (entries 13 and 14).
Studies of reaction duration found that 6 h was more e ﬃcient.
The e ﬀects of ligands on the reaction were also studied, and
found that 15 mol% of dtbbpy was optimal (see the ESI †).
Switching the photocatalyst from fac-Ir( ppy)
3 to Ir[dF(CF 3)
ppy]2(dtbbpy)PF6, 9-mesityl-10-methylacridinium perchlorate,
[Ir( ppy)2(dtbbpy)]PF6 or perylene led to lower yields, whereas
the employment of Rhodamine 6G, Ru(bpy) 3Cl2·6H2O, 4CzIPN,
thioxanthen-9-one, Ru(bpy) 3(PF6)2 and Solvent Red 43 as the
photocatalyst could not a ﬀord any of the desired product (see
the ESI †). The control experiments demonstrated that visible
light, photocatalyst and Cu catalyst were indispensable for the
reaction, while ligands and alkalis could promote the reaction
(entries 17– 22).
With the optimized reaction conditions in hand, the sub-
strate scope of the reaction was investigated (Scheme 3).
Various 1,3-enynes ( 1a–y) underwent this transformation
smoothly, providing corresponding difluoro( phenylthiol)alkyl-
ated allenes ( 3a–y) in moderate to good yields. For 2-aryl-sub-
stituted 1,3-enynes, common functional groups on the
benzene ring such as alkyl ( 1b–f ), halogen ( 1g–j), alkoxy ( 1k),
trifluoromethyl ( 1l), nitrile ( 1m), phenyl ( 1n) and benzyloxy

(1o) were well tolerated. 1,3-Enyne ( 1e) with two substituents
on the benzene ring was e ﬃciently converted to the corres-
ponding product ( 3e). In addition, pyridyl-substituted 1,3-
enyne ( 1q) was found to be a suitable substrate, a ﬀording the
target product 3q in moderate yield. 1,2,4-Trisubstituted 1,3-
enyne (1p) is also compatible with this reaction. Next, the reac-
tivity of various 1,3-enyne with di ﬀerent R 2 group were tested,
such as hexyl ( 1r), tert-butyl ( 1s), cyclopropyl ( 1t), totyl ( 1u),
cyclohexyl ( 1v), chloro ( 1w), amide ( 1x) and hydroxyalkyl ( 1y).
These substrates are tolerated, providing various allenyl
nitriles 3r–y in moderate to good yields. The difluoroalkyla-
tion-cyanation of 1,3-enynes was further investigated by switch-
ing the quaternary phosphonium reagent from 2e to (difluoro-
methyl)triphenylphosphonium bromide 2b (Scheme 4).
Fortunately, difluoromethylcyanoylated allenes 4a–y were
obtained in moderated to excellent yields (33 – 92%) under the
optimal conditions. The reactions of 1a could be easily scaled
up to 3 mmol scale, a ﬀording 3a and 4a in yield of 71% and
69%, respectively.
In order to showcase the synthetic utility of the method,
transformations of the allenyl nitriles were demonstrated
(Scheme 5). 4a could be readily converted into 6,6-difluoro-3-
iodo-4-phenylhexa-2,4-dienenitrile 5 in 65% yield with
1.5 equiv. of N-iodosuccinimide (NIS) (Scheme 5a). 24

Moreover, the bromination/cyclization of PhSCF 2-substituted
allene 3y and 4y with N-bromosuccinimide (NBS) a ﬀorded the
corresponding 3,6-dihydro-2 H-pyran-4-carbonitrile 6a and 6b
in yield of 45% and 62%, respectively. (Scheme 5b). 14,21,25
Furthermore, oxidation of 3a with m-CPBA (3-chloroperoxyben-
zoic acid) gave PhSO 2CF2-substituted allenyl nitrile 7 in 65%
yield (Scheme 5c). 26
In order to gain mechanistic insight, several preliminary
mechanistic experiments were performed. The absence of
either the photoredox catalyst fac-Ir( ppy)3 or visible light shut
down the reactivity completely, thus suggesting a crucial role
for both of these elements for the transformation (Table 1,
entries 17 and 21). The formation of desired product 3a was
completely inhibited under otherwise identical standard con-
ditions after adding a radical scavenger (TEMPO, 2,2,6,6-tetra-
methylpiperidine-1-oxyl). This result demonstrated that a
radical pathway was probably involved in this transformation.
Furthermore, a radical clock experiment with vinyl cyclopro-
pane 8 was carried out to deliver the ring opening product 9a
and 9b in yield of 85% and 84%, respectively (Scheme 6a). On
the basis of this result and literature precedents,

Firstly, photocatalyst fac-Ir( ppy)3 is excited under visible-light
irradiation. Then, single-electron transfer (SET) reduction of
phosphonium reagent 2 with fac-IrIII( ppy)3*a ﬀords difluor-
oalkyl radical A and fac-IrIV( ppy)3. Subsequently, difluoroalkyl
radicals A were added to 1,3-enyne to form allenyl radical B,
which was then isomerized to obtain radical intermediate C.
Next, allenyl radical C were combined with [ligand/Cu II(CN)]
complex F to generate [Cu III] complex G. Finally, reductive
elimination of complex G releases the desired product 3 and
regenerates the CuI catalyst.
Conclusions
In conclusion, we have developed a practical photoredox/
copper-catalyzed difluoroalkylation-cyanation of 1,3-enynes
with {difluoro( phenylthio)methyl}triphenylphosphonium tri-
flate/(difluoromethyl)triphenylphosphonium bromide and
TMSCN. This protocol provides a straightforward access to a
series of previously unknown and potentially valuable difluoro
( phenylthio)methylated and difluoromethylated allenes.
Further investigations of the applications of fluoroalkylpho-
sphonium salts in organic synthesis and medicinal chemistry
are currently underway.
